summary: Describes an experimental framework for splitting the IPv4 address space into a globally unique core space (Area Locators) and a regionally unique edge space (Endpoint Locators). It proposes a 32x32 bit addressing scheme and hierarchical routing to help address scalability. It is Experimental.

eli5.summary: Imagine street addresses with a city part that is unique everywhere and a house part that only needs to be unique locally. This proposes dividing IPv4 addresses into two such layers.

questions: ipv4 address space split core and edge
how does hipv4 reduce routing table size
what is the difference between aloc and eloc
how do realm border routers work
subtitle: Splitting IPv4 into a hierarchical core-and-edge addressing scheme for better routing scalability.

tldr.problem: The IPv4 routing system faces scalability challenges as the number of address prefixes grows, making it harder for routers to manage the global routing table efficiently.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC proposes dividing IPv4 addresses into two layers: globally unique Area Locators (ALOCs) for core routing and regionally unique Endpoint Locators (ELOCs) for edge networks, similar to how postal addresses use city codes and house numbers.
tldr.outcome: This hierarchical approach reduces the size of core routing tables and allows address reuse at network edges while remaining backward compatible with classic IPv4. However, it requires substantial network upgrades and was superseded by IPv6 and other routing solutions.

today: RFC 6306 remains Experimental and was not adopted into the Internet standards. The rapid deployment of IPv6, combined with shorter-term routing scalability solutions, reduced interest in hIPv4. However, the RFC contributed important ideas to the discussion on routing architecture and the role of hierarchical addressing in Internet scalability.

sections.title: Introduction and Motivation
sections.content:
The Internet routing table was growing rapidly in 2011, threatening the scalability of the system. Routers in the global Default-Free Zone (DFZ) had to store and process increasingly large numbers of prefixes. The hierarchical IPv4 framework (hIPv4) was proposed as an evolutionary solution that would not require replacing IPv4 with IPv6.

The framework was inspired by the LISP (Locator/Identifier Separation Protocol) approach but addresses its concerns about overlay networks and caching by introducing a peer-to-peer architecture using header swapping at border routers, similar to MPLS.
sections.eli5: Think of the problem like a phone directory that doubles in size every few years. Instead of rewriting the whole book, hIPv4 suggests splitting it into city codes and phone numbers so you only track city codes at the global level.

sections.title: Hierarchical Addressing Scheme
sections.content:
The core innovation is dividing the IPv4 address space into two categories: Area Locators (ALOCs) and Endpoint Locators (ELOCs). ALOCs are globally unique 32-bit addresses assigned to define geographic or administrative regions called ALOC realms. ELOCs are 32-bit addresses assigned to individual endpoints but are only required to be unique within their ALOC realm (or region), not globally.

This creates a 32x32 bit addressing space rather than the flat 32-bit space. An endpoint's full location is specified by the tuple of (ALOC, ELOC), allowing address reuse across different ALOC realms while keeping the core routing table manageable. The Global Locator Block (GLB) is a reserved IPv4 address space from which all ALOCs are allocated.
sections.eli5: Each address now has two parts: a global city code (ALOC) that is unique worldwide, and a local house number (ELOC) that only needs to be unique in that city. This way, many cities can use house numbers 1-1000 without conflict.

sections.title: The Locator Header
sections.content:
To implement hIPv4, a shim header called the locator header is inserted between the IPv4 header and the transport layer. This header contains optional Area Locator and Endpoint Locator fields (each 32 bits), along with control flags and a checksum. The header can be 4 bytes (for intra-realm sessions) or 12 bytes (for inter-realm sessions).

Key fields include the A-bit (indicating cross-realm traffic), I-bit (for identifier/locator split schemes), S-bit (set by border routers when swapping addresses), and FI-bits (Forwarding Indicator, controlling which routing table to use at different network stages). The design adds no visible overhead since packets are assembled at the endpoint before sending.
sections.eli5: Think of the locator header as an extra address label you write on the envelope before mailing. For local mail it is tiny; for distant cities it includes both the city code and house number plus some instructions for the post office.

sections.title: Realm Border Routers and Routing
sections.content:
Realm Border Routers (RBRs) are specialized nodes that sit at the boundary of ALOC realms. They identify hIPv4 packets, verify checksums, and swap the source and destination addresses between the IP header and the locator header. This allows routers within the DFZ to route solely on ALOCs, while edge routers within an ALOC realm can route on ELOCs.

The framework defines two main routing architectures: an intermediate phase where RBRs perform swapping as traffic crosses realm boundaries, and a long-term phase where upgraded routers avoid swapping by using the FI-bits to select the appropriate forwarding table. RBRs can also be deployed as anycast routers or with multicast support (mRBRs) to distribute traffic across multiple attachment points.
sections.eli5: Imagine post offices at city borders that rewrite envelopes: they replace the local house number with the city code for long-distance delivery, then switch it back when the mail reaches the destination city. This lets local mail carriers use simple house numbers.

sections.title: Extensions and Deployment Challenges
sections.content:
The framework requires extensions to multiple systems: DNS (to advertise ALOC information alongside addresses), the IPv4 socket API (to handle ALOC/ELOC tuples), DHCP (to provision local ALOCs), and various applications that embed IP addresses (SIP, Mobile IP, IPsec AH, ICMP, multicast protocols).

A major advantage is backward compatibility: applications and systems within a single ALOC realm do not need modification. However, applications communicating across realms must be upgraded. The framework can be deployed incrementally, with legacy systems living alongside hIPv4 systems. Concerns remain about multipath transport protocols, DDoS mitigation (since ELOC prefixes are not globally routable), and the rapid IPv4 address depletion that occurred shortly after publication.
sections.eli5: Rolling out this system requires updating phone directories (DNS), mail sorting software (routers), and how applications call home. But since local mail still works the old way, not everything needs to change at once.

fields.name: IPv4 Header (20 bytes)
fields.desc: Standard IPv4 header; destination contains ALOC for inter-realm traffic.

fields.name: A-bit
fields.desc: Set to 1 if ALOC and ELOC fields are present (inter-realm).

fields.name: I-bit
fields.desc: Set to 1 if identifier/locator split is in use.

fields.name: S-bit
fields.desc: Set by RBR when swapping source and destination addresses.

fields.name: FI-bits
fields.desc: Forwarding Indicator: controls which FIB to use (local ALOC exit, DFZ, remote ELOC approach, or multicast RPF).

fields.name: Area Locator (optional)
fields.desc: Globally unique locator for the ALOC realm.

fields.name: Endpoint Locator (optional)
fields.desc: Locally unique address of the endpoint within the ALOC realm.
